explanations.explanation: This feature detects the “express or implied” phrase in software‐license boilerplate—i.e. the standard warranty-disclaimer wording used in license headers.

This neuron is a “heading/titles” detector: it lights up on the words, numbers or punctuation that appear as top‐level labels or article/section headlines (e.g. UPDATE, News, Main menu, “10,” “18,” Reuters, etc.), signaling the start of a title or UI section.

This feature picks out relational connectors in formal, structured text—specifically the “A to B” range marker (as in “week to week”) and the “either X or Y” disjunction in license/legal boilerplate (as in “either express or implied”).

This feature fires on standalone, capitalized “label” tokens—things like menu items, section headings or UI labels, date/day abbreviations, titles and other metadata markers that mark off or title chunks of content.

This neuron is a boundary detector – it spikes on the tokens that open or close a sentence‐ or clause‐level unit (sentence‐initial content subwords like “Eureka”/“PUT(puter)” or sentence‐final punctuation, tags or delimiters).

This feature fires on the delimiters and boundary tokens that mark out file‐ or document‐level metadata/boilerplate (e.g. PHP’s “<?php”, HTML DOCTYPE or comment tags, “Generated by…” and “DO NOT EDIT” notices, copyright/license headers, version strings, article or function‐doc titles, etc.).

This feature picks up the characteristic permission‐grant and disclaimer language in open-source license headers (e.g. “Permission is hereby granted,” “distributed in the hope,” “without warranties or representations,” etc.) found in code comment blocks.
This feature fires on the last token of a standalone heading or title (e.g. news‐article headlines, section labels or menu titles), effectively marking the end‐of‐title boundary.

explanations.explanation: This unit is a boilerplate‐header detector for the “link to the license” line in Apache‐style source-file comments—specifically the phrase around “you may obtain a copy of the License at [URL]” (i.e. the “at”/punctuation/whitespace immediately before or after the license URL).

This neuron fires on the opening label of a new section or “headline” in text or code—e.g. menu or archive titles, article/post headings, patent or product titles, HTML navigation labels, C++ preprocessor directives, etc. It’s a general “start-of-section/title” detector.

This neuron fires on those byte-pair/subword tokens that begin with non-alphanumeric symbols in structured contexts—things like “=>” arrows in code, “=“ in XML attributes, the leading digit of a percentage or decimal, string/bracket delimiters, and even subword fragments like “otically.” In other words, it marks the token boundaries introduced by punctuation or symbols in code, data‐structure literals, and numeric notation.

This feature detects high-level structural markers that introduce or separate major document sections—i.e. headings and title lines or their delimiters (case-caption lines in legal briefs, DOCTYPE/html head tags, news or blog headlines, “Generated by…” and “DO NOT EDIT” comment blocks, underline/asterisk separators, etc.).

This neuron is a “subword‐junction” detector: it lights up on those tiny, high-frequency BPE pieces that glue words together—prepositional connectors (“of”), the core of mult-word comparatives (“soon,” “long,” “much” in “as soon/long/much as…”), the suffix “-able,” hyphens in compounds (“state-of-the-art”), and little consonant clusters like “qu” or “ple.” In short, it flags the small functional morphemes and punctuation marks that link or modify larger words.

This neuron lights up on the “preamble” or section‐header markers you often see at the top of code or docs—comment and markup prefixes (/* … */, //, #, %), license/author headers, include/require/import/define guards, JUnit or Roxygen tags, Markdown headings, etc.—i.e. the structural tokens that signal file‐level metadata or section boundaries.

This neuron lights up on the “meaty” part of multi‐token content words or identifiers – the subword pieces carrying real semantic load (e.g. the ‘次’ in 年次, the ‘M’ of MongoDbFactory, the ‘emb’ of embryonic, the ‘ユーザー’ in a Kubernetes add-user snippet, the Chinese ‘字体’ for font, the “Option1” label in JSON, names in titles like Attack On Titan, cancer subtypes like “大細胞,” etc.). In short, it flags the core subword of compound nouns, class‐or module names, labels and other domain‐specific content tokens.

This feature flags the standardized header block of U.S. federal appellate opinions—especially “UNPUBLISHED” Fourth (and other) Circuit rulings—capturing the “UNPUBLISHED” label, court name, case number, party captions (Plaintiff–Appellee v. Defendant–Appellant), and related procedural metadata.

This feature fires on the opening of a new structural unit or “block” boundary—whether that’s an XML/HTML tag start, a code‐declaration line (imports, class or protocol definitions, instance-var declarations), or the lead token of a standalone question (“What…”). It’s essentially a marker for the beginning of a fresh element or statement in a structured document.

This feature is a “headline‐detector” – it lights up on tokens that form the title or section‐heading of a news/article snippet (e.g. the last word of a headline or other title‐style tokens in Title Case or in quotes), marking the boundary between a headline and the following body text.

This neuron fires on the “main” numeric element or operator that defines what you’re being asked to compute in a math‐problem prompt—i.e. the final constant (or key symbol) at the end of a GCD, prime‐factorization, remainder, digit‐extraction or equation‐solving question.

This neuron is a “boundary marker” detector—it fires on tokens that open or close logical blocks and sentences/statements (e.g. comment delimiters `/*`, HTML‐tag delimiters `<…>`, statement terminators like `.` or `;`, and other punctuation that marks the end or start of a code or prose segment).

This neuron lights up on formal “structuring” tokens that introduce or separate clauses or list items in technical/legal text—e.g. the parenthesized numbers or letters (1), (2), (a), (b) that mark steps in a study or patent, and key qualifiers like “without” or “as” in license‐style provisos.

This feature marks the boundary at the end of headlines or section titles—i.e. the final word or closing punctuation of titles in news and academic texts.

explanations.explanation: This feature fires on the standard “Licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0” boilerplate in source‐code comment headers.

This feature detects the start of high‐level section or article headings—tokens that kick off titles, category labels or menu items (e.g. “Video:”, “News,” book or article titles, site navigation labels) in web and news‐style content.

This neuron fires on the little “hook” or teaser words that wrap up headlines, captions and call-to-action lines—the punchy terms (newsletter, PLC, wonder, peek, look, answer, surprise, sound, Now, etc.) you find at the end of titles, buttons or intro snippets that promise content or prod you to engage.
This neuron fires on the final, standout token of headings or titles—whether in news headlines, UI labels, section headers or code comments—marking the boundary at the end of a title-like element.

This feature lights up on small subword pieces made up of dense consonant sequences (e.g. “SK,” “CHN,” “AZZ,” “LIC,” “UNN,” “PROC,” etc.) that form the medial stems or affix‐like fragments of longer words across a variety of languages.

This neuron flags non-prose “structural” markers in web-scraped news or article text—things like section titles (“News,” “Club News,” “Main menu”), link prompts (“Read More »,” “Related Articles”), metadata labels (“FILE PHOTO:,” “TOLL FREE #”), headlines and other formatting cues that delineate page layout rather than narrative content.

This neuron lights up on the semantic “head” of a content-rich phrase—i.e. the main noun/pronoun or time/organization label that carries the phrase’s core meaning (e.g. “form,” “Explorer,” “you,” “Oct,” “1998,” “Center”).
This feature detects sentence-final punctuation—the period/full-stop (including ideographic “。”) that marks the end of a statement across different languages and scripts.

This feature is essentially a “full-stop” detector: it fires on the period (and similar boundary tokens) that mark ends of sentences, headings or abbreviations (e.g. the “.” in U.S., patent‐claim endings, headline breaks, etc.).

This neuron fires whenever the model reaches the *end* of a tightly-delimited expression or statement—i.e. the closing parenthesis/bracket/brace (often with its trailing semicolon or punctuation) that marks the boundary of a code or math fragment.

This neuron fires on discourse-level “signal” words that mark negation, contrast or exception (negative contractions like don’t/doesn’t/isn’t/wasn’t/hasn’t, etc.) and other transition markers that introduce emphasis or examples (however, for example, more importantly, majority).

This feature flags the boundary‐marking tokens (dots, blank lines or punctuation) that separate one formal section or block from the next in structured documents—e.g. the period in a DOI, the blank line before a Reuters credit or court-case heading, or the newline before a new problem statement.

This feature fires on cardinal numerals that encode a quantity or scale (e.g. “more than 60 000 members,” “over 40 000 fans,” “1500 students,” “4000 years,” “300 000 civilians,” etc.) in factual or encyclopedic contexts. It thus abstracts the notion “numeric count/statistic” in descriptive prose.
This feature detects the “dot” punctuation token (.)—whether as a sentence terminator, acronym separator (e.g. “U.S.”), decimal point or in file‐extension contexts (e.g. “.tif”).

This feature detects the “**” delimiter – the double‐asterisk token used across UI text and code for emphasis or section breaks (e.g. markdown bold markers, doc-block comment headers, registration prompts and headings).

This feature detects the tokens that kick off new top-level entries or headers in highly structured text—whether it’s an “include” or “import” line in code, an “Atty” label in a court opinion’s counsel list, or the name of a district in a Wikipedia‐style rundown of place names. It essentially marks the start of each item in those domain-specific lists or declarations.
